correctness.rationale: Shattering four points would put all four in one radius-one ball. A coordinate line has only full-line, singleton or empty intersections with such balls, so a shattered four-set must use more than one line through the all-positive center. There are then three arms across at least two coordinates. If two share a line, their common centers lie on that line and only the all-positive center also reaches the third. If three use different coordinates, the first two have exactly two common centers, and the third excludes the double-change center. Thus the three-arm proper trace is impossible. The binary-cube triple realizes all eight traces, including the empty one via a triple-coordinate change; fixing other coordinates preserves all distances. In a rectangle all-positive triples lie in a row/column cross; a collinear triple loses pair traces and an L loses the corner singleton. The remaining shape occupies two rows and three columns (up to transpose), so the empty trace forces one spare row and column. The explicit witnesses work at 3x4 and above, and the same-row pair works outside 2x2 whenever the formula needs dimension two. The one-coordinate and 2x2 degeneracies follow from constant and co-singleton concepts respectively.
residual_risks: Independent unanchored finite checks verified the boundary rectangles 3x3 and 3x4 and representative products, including binary cubes in dimensions three and four. Universal coverage instead rests on the exact intersection and cross arguments.

evidence: The rook-graph result classifies and counts all shattered supports in two coordinates, not just the maximum sizes. Coudert–Csikós–Ducoffe–Viennot give general closed-graph algorithms and size, degree, degeneracy and matching bounds. Housholder–Mangiapanello–Senger address open-neighborhood shattering in subsets.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The rook specialization yields the full two-factor part. Generic closed bounds or open results alone do not give the heterogeneous closed classification.
